about: The interior of the heart: its four chambers, the septa, the four valves, the lumens of the great vessels, the coronary arteries, the conduction system and the pericardium, drawn inside the glass shell of the organ. Chamber size, valve state, blood colour and the beat-by-beat spread of the electrical impulse follow the simulation's own cardiac cycle. Many parts hold finer structures of their own (papillary muscles and chordae tendineae in a ventricle, the cusps of a valve, the branches of a coronary artery, the layers of the pericardium): select a part, or zoom in on it, and they appear inside it; the Structures list nests them under their parent. The shapes are adult-mean drawings, not anyone's scan, and the cusps, cords and ridges are schematic: their number and layout are illustrative. Activity is a display index of how hard the model's drives are pushing a structure; a structure with no drive of its own shows its parent's. It is not a measurement and nothing here is clinical advice.

GH14.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed. Elsevier, 2021.

GRAYS42.label: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

parts.label: Right Atrium
parts.summary: Receives deoxygenated blood from the body
parts.function: The right atrium collects blood returning from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae and passes it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Most filling is passive, with a small extra push from atrial contraction at the end of diastole. In this simulator it is drawn in the colour of venous blood and swells and shrinks with its live volume.

drives.note: A faster rate means more atrial contractions each minute.
Atrial fibrillation replaces organised contraction with chaotic electrical activity.
With no organised output the chamber does no useful work.

parts.label: Right Ventricle
parts.summary: Pumps blood to the lungs
parts.function: The right ventricle is a thin-walled crescent wrapped round the front of the septum. It receives blood through the tricuspid valve and ejects it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, against the low resistance of the lungs. It brightens with each beat and with a stronger or faster heart.

drives.note: More beats per minute means more ejections.
Stronger contractility raises the work of each beat.
Weaker contractility lowers the work done.
No organised beat means no pumping.

parts.label: Left Atrium
parts.summary: Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs
parts.function: The left atrium lies at the back of the heart and receives oxygenated blood from the four pulmonary veins. It empties through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, adding a final push at the end of diastole. It is drawn in the colour of arterial blood, so a hypoxic body visibly darkens it.

drives.note: A faster rate means more atrial contractions each minute.
Atrial fibrillation replaces organised contraction with chaotic electrical activity.
With no organised output the chamber does no useful work.

parts.label: Left Ventricle
parts.summary: Pumps blood to the whole body
parts.function: The left ventricle has the thickest wall of the four chambers because it must drive blood round the entire systemic circulation. It fills through the mitral valve and ejects through the aortic valve into the aorta, and the apex points down, forward and to the left. Its cavity shrinks sharply in systole and refills slowly in diastole.

drives.note: More beats per minute means more ejections.
Stronger contractility raises the work of each beat.
Weaker contractility lowers the work done.
No organised beat means no pumping.

parts.label: Interventricular Septum
parts.summary: Muscular wall between the two ventricles
parts.function: The septum separates the right and left ventricles so that deoxygenated and oxygenated blood never mix. It is mostly muscle, shares in the contraction of the left ventricle, and carries the bundle branches of the conduction system. It brightens as the heart works harder.

drives.note: The septum contracts with every beat, so a faster rate means more work.
With no organised beat it does no work.

parts.label: Tricuspid Valve
parts.summary: Three-cusped valve, right atrium to right ventricle
parts.function: The tricuspid valve lets blood pass from the right atrium to the right ventricle during diastole and closes when the ventricle contracts, so blood is not forced backwards. In the interior view it fades and shrinks towards its ring when open and returns when closed.

drives.note: The valve opens and closes once per beat, so it works more at a faster rate.
With no organised beat the valve is not cycling.

parts.label: Mitral Valve
parts.summary: Two-cusped valve, left atrium to left ventricle
parts.function: The mitral valve lets oxygenated blood flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle in diastole and shuts firmly when the ventricle contracts against the high pressure of the systemic circulation. It is open in diastole and closed in systole.

drives.note: The valve opens and closes once per beat, so it works more at a faster rate.
With no organised beat the valve is not cycling.

parts.label: Pulmonary Valve
parts.summary: Semilunar valve at the root of the pulmonary trunk
parts.function: The pulmonary valve opens when the right ventricle ejects and closes at the end of systole, stopping blood from falling back into the ventricle. It is the reverse of the atrioventricular valves: open in systole, closed in diastole.

drives.note: The valve opens and closes once per beat, so it works more at a faster rate.
With no organised beat the valve is not cycling.

parts.label: Aortic Valve
parts.summary: Semilunar valve at the root of the aorta
parts.function: The aortic valve opens while the left ventricle ejects and closes as it relaxes, which keeps the arterial pressure from draining back into the heart. In this simulator it is shown open only while the engine's aortic flow is positive.

drives.note: The valve opens and closes once per beat, so it works more at a faster rate.
With no organised beat the valve is not cycling.

parts.label: Ascending Aorta
parts.summary: Carries oxygenated blood out of the left ventricle
parts.function: The ascending aorta rises from the aortic valve and carries oxygenated blood into the arch and on to the whole body. Its wall stretches with each ejection and recoils to keep flow going in diastole. It brightens when the cardiac output rises or the arterial pressure is high.

drives.note: More blood is ejected through it per minute.
Higher arterial pressure loads the wall.
Less blood is ejected through it per minute.

parts.label: Pulmonary Trunk
parts.summary: Carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs
parts.function: The pulmonary trunk rises from the right ventricle and divides into the pulmonary arteries that take deoxygenated blood to the lungs. It carries the same volume per minute as the aorta, at much lower pressure. It is drawn in the colour of venous blood.

drives.note: The right ventricle ejects the same output as the left.
Less blood is ejected through it per minute.

parts.label: Venae Cavae
parts.summary: Bring blood from the body back to the heart
parts.function: The superior vena cava drains the head, neck and arms, and the inferior vena cava drains the trunk and legs. Both empty into the right atrium, and the flow they deliver is the venous return that sets how much the heart can eject. They are drawn in the colour of venous blood and dim when blood volume falls.

drives.note: A higher cardiac output requires a higher venous return.
A smaller blood volume reduces venous return.

parts.label: Pulmonary Veins
parts.summary: Four veins bringing oxygenated blood from the lungs
parts.function: Two pulmonary veins from each lung bring newly oxygenated blood into the back of the left atrium. They are unusual among veins in carrying oxygenated blood. They are drawn in the colour of arterial blood.

drives.note: A higher cardiac output requires a higher return from the lungs.
A lower cardiac output means a lower return from the lungs.

parts.label: Coronary Arteries
parts.summary: Supply the heart muscle itself with blood
parts.function: The left main coronary artery divides into the anterior interventricular branch, which runs down the front groove towards the apex, and the circumflex, which curves round the left atrioventricular groove. The right coronary artery runs round the right groove. Left coronary flow is squeezed off while the ventricle contracts and occurs mainly in diastole. They brighten as the heart works harder or its muscle is short of oxygen.

drives.note: A faster heart needs more blood to its muscle.
Stronger contraction raises the oxygen demand of the muscle.
A shortage of oxygen in the muscle is a stimulus for coronary vasodilation.

parts.label: Sinoatrial Node
parts.summary: The heart's natural pacemaker
parts.function: The sinoatrial node sits in the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava and sets the heart rate. Sympathetic activity speeds it up and vagal activity slows it. In the interior view it flashes about a fifth of a second before each ventricular beat.

drives.note: The node fires faster as the rate rises.
Sympathetic outflow speeds the pacemaker.
A slower rate means slower node firing.

parts.label: Atrioventricular Node
parts.summary: Delays the impulse between atria and ventricles
parts.function: The atrioventricular node lies low in the wall between the two atria. It slows the impulse briefly so that the atria finish emptying before the ventricles begin to contract. In the interior view it glows after the sinoatrial node and just before the bundle of His.

drives.note: The node conducts once per beat, so it is used more at a faster rate.

parts.label: Bundle of His and Purkinje Fibres
parts.summary: Fast conduction fibres through the ventricles
parts.function: The bundle of His runs down the septum and divides into right and left bundle branches, which spread into fine Purkinje fibres over the ventricular walls. This fast network lets the ventricles contract almost together. In the interior view a bright impulse sweeps down it at the start of each ventricular beat, and it is disorganised in fibrillation.

drives.note: The network conducts once per beat, so it is used more at a faster rate.
Fibrillation makes the electrical activity chaotic and continuous.

parts.label: Interatrial Septum
parts.summary: Wall between the two atria
parts.function: The interatrial septum separates the right atrium from the left atrium, so that venous and oxygenated blood do not mix at atrial level. On its right-atrial face it carries a shallow oval depression, the fossa ovalis, which marks where the foramen ovale of the fetal heart closed. Open the septum to see it.

drives.note: The septum moves with every atrial beat, so a faster rate means more work.
With no organised beat it does no work.

parts.label: Pericardium
parts.summary: The sac that holds the heart
parts.function: The pericardium is the double-walled sac in which the heart lies. A tough outer fibrous layer anchors it to its surroundings, and inside that a thin serous membrane folds back on itself: one layer lines the sac and the other covers the heart. A film of lubricating fluid between them lets the heart move with each beat with little friction. It is drawn here as a faint glass envelope; open it to see its layers.

parts.label: Papillary Muscles (left)
parts.summary: Muscular columns that anchor the mitral cords
parts.function: Two columns of muscle, the anterolateral and the posteromedial papillary muscles, rise from the inner wall of the left ventricle. They contract with the ventricle and keep the cords tight, which stops the mitral cusps being pushed back into the left atrium when the ventricle squeezes.

drives.note: Each beat tenses them, so a faster rate means more work.
Stronger contraction raises the load on the muscle.
Weaker contraction lowers the work done.
No organised beat means no contraction.

parts.label: Chordae Tendineae (left)
parts.summary: Fine cords from the papillary muscles to the mitral cusps
parts.function: The chordae tendineae are thin fibrous cords that run from the tips of the papillary muscles to the free edges of the mitral cusps. They hold the cusps shut against the pressure of systole, like the guy-ropes of a tent. They are passive tissue, so here they simply show the activity of the ventricle they belong to.

parts.label: Trabeculae Carneae (left)
parts.summary: Muscular ridges on the inner wall
parts.function: The inner surface of the left ventricle is not smooth: it is raised into ridges and bridges of muscle called trabeculae carneae. Some are fixed along their length, some are attached only at their ends, and the papillary muscles are the largest of the free-standing type. The wall near the outflow tract is smooth.

parts.label: Papillary Muscles (right)
parts.summary: Muscular columns that anchor the tricuspid cords
parts.function: The right ventricle has an anterior, a posterior and a septal papillary muscle. As in the left ventricle they contract with the chamber and keep the cords tight so that the tricuspid cusps do not blow back into the right atrium in systole.

drives.note: Each beat tenses them, so a faster rate means more work.
Stronger contraction raises the load on the muscle.
Weaker contraction lowers the work done.
No organised beat means no contraction.

parts.label: Chordae Tendineae (right)
parts.summary: Fine cords from the papillary muscles to the tricuspid cusps
parts.function: Thin fibrous cords join the tips of the right papillary muscles to the edges of the three tricuspid cusps, and each muscle sends cords to more than one cusp. They are passive tissue, so here they show the activity of the right ventricle.

parts.label: Trabeculae Carneae (right)
parts.summary: Muscular ridges and the septomarginal band
parts.function: The inner wall of the right ventricle is more coarsely ridged than that of the left. One thick band, the septomarginal trabecula (the moderator band), crosses the cavity from the septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle and carries part of the right bundle branch.

parts.label: Anterior Mitral Cusp
parts.summary: The larger cusp, next to the aortic outflow
parts.function: The anterior cusp of the mitral valve lies between the inflow and the outflow of the left ventricle, next to the aortic valve. It is the larger of the two cusps and, with the posterior cusp, closes the orifice in systole. Its edge is tethered by cords from both papillary muscles.

parts.label: Posterior Mitral Cusp
parts.summary: The cusp on the free wall side
parts.function: The posterior cusp of the mitral valve is attached along most of the circumference of the orifice, on the side of the free wall of the left ventricle. It meets the anterior cusp along a line of closure when the ventricle contracts.

parts.label: Anterior Tricuspid Cusp
parts.summary: The cusp facing the front of the ventricle
parts.function: The anterior cusp of the tricuspid valve is generally the largest of the three. It faces the front of the right ventricle, and its edge is held by cords from the anterior papillary muscle among others.

parts.label: Posterior Tricuspid Cusp
parts.summary: The cusp facing the back of the ventricle
parts.function: The posterior cusp of the tricuspid valve lies along the lower, back wall of the right ventricle. It closes the orifice together with the other two cusps in systole.

parts.label: Septal Tricuspid Cusp
parts.summary: The cusp on the septum side
parts.function: The septal cusp of the tricuspid valve lies against the interventricular septum. It is held by cords, some of which come from the septal wall itself.

parts.label: Right Coronary Cusp
parts.summary: Aortic cusp over the right coronary artery
parts.function: The aortic valve has three semilunar cusps. The right coronary cusp lies in front, and the right coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it. Each cusp is a pocket that fills with blood and seals the valve when the ventricle relaxes.

parts.label: Left Coronary Cusp
parts.summary: Aortic cusp over the left coronary artery
parts.function: The left coronary cusp lies to the left of the aortic valve, and the left main coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it. Its pocket fills with blood and closes against the other two cusps in diastole.

parts.label: Non-coronary Cusp
parts.summary: Aortic cusp with no coronary artery behind it
parts.function: The non-coronary cusp lies at the back of the aortic valve, next to the interatrial septum. No coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it.

parts.label: Anterior Pulmonary Cusp
parts.summary: Pulmonary cusp at the front
parts.function: The pulmonary valve has three semilunar cusps. The anterior cusp lies at the front of the valve. Like the aortic cusps it is a pocket that fills with blood and seals the valve when the right ventricle relaxes.

parts.label: Left Pulmonary Cusp
parts.summary: Pulmonary cusp on the left
parts.function: The left cusp of the pulmonary valve lies on the patient’s left. It closes against its two neighbours when the right ventricle relaxes.

parts.label: Right Pulmonary Cusp
parts.summary: Pulmonary cusp on the right
parts.function: The right cusp of the pulmonary valve lies on the patient’s right. It closes against its two neighbours when the right ventricle relaxes.

parts.label: Muscular Septum
parts.summary: The thick muscular part of the septum
parts.function: Most of the interventricular septum is muscle, and it bulges towards the right ventricle. It contracts with the left ventricle and carries the left and right bundle branches on its two faces.

parts.label: Membranous Septum
parts.summary: The small fibrous part under the aortic valve
parts.function: Near the top of the septum, just below the aortic valve, there is a small thin area of fibrous tissue instead of muscle: the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is the usual site of ventricular septal defects.

parts.label: Fossa Ovalis
parts.summary: Oval depression on the right side of the atrial septum
parts.function: The fossa ovalis is a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum, seen from the right atrium. It marks where the foramen ovale was open in the fetus, letting blood pass from the right atrium to the left before birth. In many people a slit-like channel remains at its edge.

parts.label: Left Main Coronary Artery
parts.summary: Short trunk of the left coronary artery
parts.function: The left main coronary artery arises from the aorta above the left coronary cusp and runs a short way before dividing into the left anterior descending and the circumflex arteries.

parts.label: Left Anterior Descending Artery
parts.summary: Runs down the front groove towards the apex
parts.function: The left anterior descending artery, also called the anterior interventricular branch, runs in the groove between the two ventricles on the front of the heart and down towards the apex. It gives branches to the front of the left ventricle and to the septum.

parts.label: Circumflex Artery
parts.summary: Curves round the left side of the heart
parts.function: The circumflex artery runs in the groove between the left atrium and the left ventricle, round the left border of the heart to its back. It supplies the left atrium and much of the side and back of the left ventricle.

parts.label: Right Coronary Artery
parts.summary: Runs in the groove on the right side
parts.function: The right coronary artery arises from the aorta above the right coronary cusp and runs in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle, round the right border to the back of the heart. It supplies the right atrium and ventricle, and commonly the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.

parts.label: Posterior Descending Artery
parts.summary: Runs in the groove on the underside
parts.function: The posterior descending artery, or posterior interventricular branch, runs in the groove between the ventricles on the underside of the heart. In most people it comes from the right coronary artery, and it supplies the back part of the septum.

parts.label: Coronary Sinus
parts.summary: Main vein that drains the heart muscle
parts.function: The coronary sinus is a wide vein that lies in the groove at the back of the heart between the left atrium and ventricle. It collects blood from the cardiac veins that drain the heart muscle and empties it into the right atrium. It carries deoxygenated blood and is drawn in the venous colour.

drives.note: More work by the muscle means more blood passing out through its veins.
Stronger contraction raises the flow through the muscle.

parts.label: Bundle of His
parts.summary: Carries the impulse from the AV node into the septum
parts.function: The bundle of His is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles. It leaves the atrioventricular node, passes through the fibrous tissue between the chambers and runs along the septum before dividing into the right and left bundle branches.

parts.label: Left Bundle Branch
parts.summary: Spreads the impulse over the left ventricle
parts.function: The left bundle branch runs down the left face of the septum and spreads into fascicles that reach the left ventricular wall and its papillary muscles.

parts.label: Right Bundle Branch
parts.summary: Carries the impulse down the right side of the septum
parts.function: The right bundle branch runs down the right face of the septum, through the septomarginal band, and reaches the free wall of the right ventricle.

parts.label: Purkinje Fibres
parts.summary: Fine fibres that carry the impulse through the ventricular wall
parts.function: The bundle branches end in a network of Purkinje fibres beneath the inner lining of the ventricles. They conduct quickly, so the ventricles contract almost together. The network is disorganised in fibrillation.

drives.note: The network conducts once per beat, so it is used more at a faster rate.
Fibrillation makes the electrical activity chaotic and continuous.

parts.label: Fibrous Pericardium
parts.summary: Tough outer layer of the sac
parts.function: The fibrous pericardium is the strong outer layer of the sac. It is attached to the diaphragm below and blends with the walls of the great vessels above, which anchors the heart in the chest and limits how far it can stretch.

parts.label: Parietal Serous Pericardium
parts.summary: Slippery membrane lining the inside of the sac
parts.function: The parietal layer of the serous pericardium is a thin, smooth membrane stuck to the inside of the fibrous layer. At the roots of the great vessels it turns back on itself to become the visceral layer.

parts.label: Epicardium (Visceral Pericardium)
parts.summary: Thin membrane on the surface of the heart
parts.function: The visceral layer of the serous pericardium, also called the epicardium, covers the outer surface of the heart muscle and the roots of the great vessels. The space between it and the parietal layer, the pericardial cavity, holds a thin film of fluid that lets the two slide over each other.
